inst.intro: The 139 university, school and department policies for students merge 2,861 statements from 301 universities, and 99 of the 139 apply while students work. The other stages hold few policies, with 2 before the course, 6 at its start, 3 during assessment, 12 when misuse is suspected and 2 over time; another 15 state background facts. By stance, No position is the largest group with 43 policies, followed by Only listed uses with 34 and Allowed with conditions with 33. Only 9 policies prohibit AI, 10 encourage it, 8 require something when AI is used, and 2 leave the decision to the instructor.

stances.prohibit: The 9 prohibitions are stated by 119 universities, and 7 of them apply while students work. The most widespread forbids students to present AI-generated work as their own (P19.04), a rule stated by 94 universities in 132 statements. The others name particular dishonest uses, such as fabricating information or concealing AI use (P36.03, 16 universities), fabricating data, citations or evidence (P74.02, 12 universities) and forging records such as medical excuses (P74.15, 3 universities). One prohibition applies during assessment and treats unauthorized notes, devices or outside resources in an exam as cheating (P22.03, 9 universities), and no prohibition applies before the course, at its start, when misuse is suspected or over time.
stances.restrict: The 34 Only listed uses policies, stated by 188 universities, limit how students use AI as they work (27 of the 34) and what they may put into AI tools. The 2 most widespread ask students to use AI to support their learning without using it as a shortcut or replacement (P32.03, 71 universities) and to keep personal, confidential or sensitive information out of AI tools (P50.06, 59 universities). Others ask students to understand everything they submit (P30.02, 24 universities), to use university-approved tools signed in with their university account (P92.06, 23 universities), and to keep course materials out of AI tools unless the instructor permits it (P49.04, 18 universities). When misuse is suspected, 70 universities state that students may not submit AI-generated content without acknowledging it (P36.09) and 13 that misuse can bring disciplinary action up to expulsion (P37.07); the only policy before the course asks students to get advisor or committee approval before using AI in theses or research (P62.03, 13 universities).
stances.permit: Of the 33 Allowed with conditions policies, stated by 146 universities, 29 apply while students work, and the most widespread make disclosure the condition. Researchers disclose and cite AI in research outputs, theses and proposals (P62.06, 46 universities), and students follow their instructor's requirements for citing AI (P24.08, 27 universities) or cite it in a style such as APA or MLA (P25.07, 24 universities). A second group allows AI as a study aid, for generating practice questions and flashcards (P14.02, 36 universities), as a tutor or role-play partner (P14.04, 12 universities) and for exam preparation (P14.05, 11 universities), while some uses need the instructor's permission, such as summarizing readings (P105.06, 6 universities) and brainstorming (P15.07, 5 universities). The only policy at the start of the course lets students use AI when the instructor gives no AI statement, provided they disclose all use (P06.05, 1 university).
stances.encourage: Three of the 10 Encourage policies teach students how to prompt, and they include the 2 most widespread: students refine their prompts through trial and error (P93.03, 14 universities) and write clear, specific prompts that give context (P93.05, 10 universities); the third asks them to break complex tasks into parts (P93.07, 4 universities). Other policies invite uses beyond assignments, such as planning study schedules (P14.07, 4 universities) and preparing for careers (P119.02, 3 universities). The 10 are stated by 35 universities in all; 8 apply while students work, and none applies before the course, at its start, during assessment or when misuse is suspected.
stances.require: The most widespread of the 8 Require policies, stated by 50 universities, asks students to check that sources and citations produced by AI exist and are accurate (P31.04, 30 universities). Each of the others is stated by 16 or fewer universities, and several concern records of AI use: 16 universities report that some instructors require logs or reflections on AI use (P26.15), and 3 ask students to write in Google Docs or Office so that their editing history can be viewed (P40.06). None of the 8 applies during assessment or when misuse is suspected.
stances.delegates: The 2 Instructor decides policies are stated by 181 of the 301 universities. Students follow the AI rules their instructor sets for each course and assignment (P78.06, 104 universities), and they check each course's expectations because AI rules differ across courses and instructors (P04.13, 120 universities).
stances.none: The 43 No position policies are stated by 281 universities and include the 2 most widely stated policies in this part. Students are told to ask their instructor when unsure whether AI use is allowed (P10.04, 193 universities, 386 statements), and they are warned that AI output can be inaccurate, biased or fabricated (P31.12, 162 universities) and that AI use can bypass the practice through which they learn (P41.08, 64 universities). Of the 12 policies for when misuse is suspected, 9 take no position; they send AI violations through existing academic integrity processes (P36.06, 75 universities), name grade penalties (P37.05, 18 universities) and describe appeals (P64.02, 7 universities). At the start of the course, 57 universities ask students to read the syllabus and assignment instructions to learn what AI use is allowed (P78.02).

course.intro: The 184 CS course policies merge 1,564 statements from syllabi at 132 universities, and 163 of the 184 apply while students work. No course policy applies before the course or states background facts, and the remaining stages hold 6 policies at the start of the course, 10 during assessment, 2 when misuse is suspected and 3 over time. The stances Prohibit (46 policies), Require (43), Allowed with conditions (42) and Only listed uses (38) are close in size. Encourage (5 policies) and No position (10) are small, and no course policy falls under Instructor decides.

stances.prohibit: Of the 46 Prohibit policies, stated by 111 universities, 40 apply while students work, and the most widespread ban AI from producing the code students submit. Students may not ask AI for answers, solutions or code for graded assignments (CT17.c03, 50 universities), submit AI-generated code or text as their own (CT17.c02, 38 universities), or use coding assistants and autocomplete such as Copilot (CT20.c02, 25 universities). Some courses ban AI outright, either for any purpose from the start of the course (CT01.c02, 21 universities) or on all graded work (CT01.c01, 23 universities), and smaller groups extend bans to learning uses such as debugging their own code (CT17.c05, 8 universities) and using AI as a tutor (CT08.c07, 3 universities). During assessment, 30 universities forbid AI on exams and quizzes (CT34.c01).
stances.restrict: The 38 Only listed uses policies, stated by 78 universities, allow AI only for uses the course names, and 36 of them apply while students work. The most widespread allows AI only when the instructor or assignment explicitly permits it (CT04.c01, 23 universities); others ask students to use AI to support their learning without replacing it (CT40.c08, 14 universities) or their own thinking (CT32.c04, 14 universities), and to use it only as they would a friend or classmate (CT33.c01, 8 universities). A few set limits on code, such as keeping code taken from AI to a few lines (CT18.c03, 4 universities) and avoiding AI interactions that produce solution code (CT19.c03, 3 universities), and 4 universities tell students to assume AI is not allowed when an assignment says nothing about it (CT05.c01). The 2 policies during assessment come from 1 university each and bar IDEs on exams (CT35.c11) or give a zero when a test answer can be found on the internet (CT35.c10).
stances.permit: The most widespread of the 42 Allowed with conditions policies, stated by 83 universities, lets students ask AI to explain course concepts and material (CT08.c01, 39 universities, 69 statements). Other permitted uses support study and the student's own code, such as exam study and practice problems (CT13.c01, 10 universities), review of code students wrote themselves (CT10.c01, 10 universities) and explanations of code, syntax and error messages (CT08.c02, 8 universities); 7 universities allow AI to interpret error messages but not to supply the fix (CT09.c01). Broader permissions let students use AI on coursework in general (CT02.c04, 15 universities) or as they see fit without asking (CT02.c05, 6 universities). At the start of the course, policies make AI optional (CT47.c01, 5 universities) and say students need not pay for AI tools (CT46.c07, 2 universities), and no Allowed with conditions policy applies during assessment.
stances.encourage: Of the 5 Encourage policies, stated by 36 universities, the most widespread welcomes students to use AI in the course (CT02.c01, 16 universities) and is the only one at the start of the course. The other 4 apply while students work. They ask students to seek help from course staff instead of from AI (CT06.c04, 14 universities), invite them to share their AI experiences (OTHER.c17, 5 universities), ask them to reflect on whether AI helped or limited their learning (CT28.c01, 3 universities), and encourage them to use coding agents as learning tools (CT21.c05, 1 university).
stances.require: Of the 43 Require policies, stated by 84 universities, 26 set what students must disclose or record when they use AI. The most widespread asks students to disclose or cite any AI use, permitted use included (CT25.c01, 40 universities), and others name the record, such as the prompts (CT27.c01, 14 universities), the full conversation transcript (CT27.c02, 8 universities) or the exact lines AI generated (CT26.c02, 7 universities). A second group makes students accountable for what they submit; they must be able to explain all code they submit (CT30.c02, 31 universities) and must verify AI output before using it (CT31.c01, 24 universities). A few policies require AI use itself, such as projects built around AI coding agents (CT21.c01, 2 universities) and a paid Claude Pro subscription (CT46.c06, 1 university).
stances.none: The 10 No position policies are stated by 41 universities, and 31 of those 41 ask students to check with course staff when unsure whether an AI use or tool is allowed (CT06.c01). Each of the other policies comes from 5 or fewer universities, for example a warning to be cautious with AI and understand its limits (CT42.c06, 5 universities), a note that students who used no AI need not submit a form (CT25.c06, 2 universities) and permission to tell staff when the policy disallows something that should be allowed (CT06.c07, 1 university).

inst.intro: The institutional documents yield 266 policies that address instructors, merged from 5,590 statements at 303 universities. Policies cluster early in the course: 103 apply before it and 56 at its start, against 43 while students work, 12 during assessment and 10 over time; another 36 address suspected misuse and 6 give background facts. Over half of the policies, 152 of 266, take no position on AI and instead set duties, such as including an AI statement in the syllabus. Of the rest, 46 allow AI only for listed uses, 34 encourage it, 20 allow it with conditions, 8 leave the decision to the instructor, and 3 each prohibit AI or require something when it is used. Although only 8 policies leave the decision to the instructor, 252 of the 303 universities state at least one of them, and only the No position policies, at 282 universities, reach more.

stances.prohibit: Two of the 3 prohibiting policies apply before the course, and both concern students' work: instructors make clear that only original, personal work counts for assessment (P29.01, 6 universities), and 1 university asks instructors in writing-intensive courses to assign writing that students complete without generative AI (P01.02). The third, also from 1 university, forbids instructors from presenting AI-generated content as their own original work (P74.05).
stances.restrict: The 46 policies that allow AI only for listed uses appear at every stage except Over time, and the most widespread of them concern detection tools. When misuse is suspected, instructors should not treat a detector result as the only evidence of misconduct (P69.02, 63 universities), and 58 universities tell instructors not to run student work through detectors at all (P39.03). Others concern student data and approved tools: while students work, instructors keep student work and identifiable information out of AI tools unless the student consents or the tool is approved (P50.08, 39 universities), and before the course they choose only approved or university-licensed tools (P92.01, 27 universities). At assessment, instructors keep a human accountable for AI-assisted grades (P46.09, 18 universities) or do not use AI to grade at all (P46.03, 17 universities), and 13 universities ask them to move exams to in-person, supervised formats (P33.04).
stances.permit: The most widespread policies that allow AI with conditions concern instructors' own use of it. Before the course, instructors may use AI to draft and refine syllabi, rubrics, quiz questions and other course materials (P59.01), a policy stated by 50 universities in 114 statements. While students work, instructors may use approved tools to draft feedback or score work against a rubric (P59.05, 16 universities), and 6 universities add that instructors must personalize AI-drafted feedback (P101.05); when misuse is suspected, they may use detector results only as preliminary or supporting evidence (P69.05, 17 universities). Other policies let instructors allow students to use AI for listed purposes, such as study aids and practice exams (P14.01, 7 universities) or editing and proofreading (P91.01, 6 universities).
stances.encourage: Of the 34 policies that encourage AI, 17 apply while students work, and none applies during assessment. Before the course, instructors are asked to design assignments that build in student AI use (P79.01), stated by 64 universities, more than any other encouraging policy, and to run their own assignments through AI tools to see how AI handles them (P63.04, 37 universities). While students work, instructors teach students how AI works and what it can and cannot do (P44.04, 45 universities), teach them to use it ethically (P44.06, 35 universities), and assign them to critique or verify AI output (P31.08, 28 universities). Only 3 encouraging policies apply over time, each stated by 3 or fewer universities, such as sharing AI assignments and syllabus statements with colleagues (P63.16, 3 universities).
stances.require: Instructors may require students to submit their prompts, transcripts, drafts or process reflections (P26.03, 43 universities, 67 statements), and may require them to disclose, cite or explain their AI use (P24.01, 32 universities). The third requiring policy, from 2 universities, has advisory committees attest to the authenticity of a student's work and AI disclosure (P62.21).
stances.delegates: Although only 8 policies leave the AI decision to the instructor, they include the most widespread of all 266 policies. At the start of the course, instructors tell students clearly whether and how they may use AI (P09.03), a policy stated by 193 universities in 389 statements. Before the course, instructors write a course AI policy (P04.02, 82 universities), which they may adapt from sample syllabus statements (P110.02, 72 universities), and while students work they state AI expectations for each assignment (P09.09, 85 universities). The only such policy for suspected misuse leaves the consequences to the instructor's discretion (P37.08, 16 universities).
stances.none: The 152 policies with no position set duties for instructors or state facts, and 63 of them apply before the course. The most widespread of those concern assessment design: instructors base AI decisions on the course's learning objectives (P83.01, 71 universities), redesign assignments and assessments in response to generative AI (P35.01, 58 universities), and assess students' learning process along with the final product (P35.02, 49 universities). The 40 policies at the start of the course concern telling students the rules, led by including a generative AI statement in the syllabus (P09.02, 191 universities, 323 statements) and explaining how to cite or acknowledge AI use (P24.03, 83 universities); 62 universities also ask instructors to tell students whether and how they use AI themselves (P47.01). The 28 policies for suspected misuse ask instructors to talk with the student in a supportive way before escalating (P57.01, 66 universities) and to report suspected misuse promptly to the academic integrity office (P81.03, 57 universities), and 47 universities say instructors may use detection or plagiarism tools (P40.07). Few apply later in the course: 8 while students work, 2 during assessment and 7 over time. The most widespread of these ask instructors to check AI output they produce and remain responsible for it (P31.05, 44 universities) and to remind students of the policy through the semester (P66.13, 35 universities).

course.intro: CS course syllabi say little about instructors. Across 19 universities, they yield 13 policies that address instructors, merged from 30 statements, compared with 266 policies from 5,590 statements in the institutional documents. The largest group, 5 of the 13, gives background facts, no other stage has more than 2 policies, and no course policy applies over time. By stance, 6 of the 13 take no position, 2 allow AI with conditions, 2 require something, and 1 each prohibits AI, allows it only for listed uses or encourages it; none leaves the decision to the instructor. Some are commitments the syllabus makes about the instructor's own conduct, such as never using AI to grade.

stances.prohibit: Syllabi at 1 university state that the instructor will never use AI to grade (OTHER.c03), the only course policy that applies during assessment.
stances.restrict: Syllabi at 1 university state, in 3 statements, that individual instructors may disallow AI entirely for assignments (CT04.c02).
stances.permit: The more widespread of the 2 policies lets instructors permit AI or grant exceptions for specific assignments (CT04.c03, 6 universities, 10 statements). The other, from 1 university, allows exceptions to the AI policy only in approved circumstances, with accommodations decided case by case (CT47.c04).
stances.encourage: At 1 university, the instructor encourages students to use AI to deepen their understanding and review difficult material (CT08.c04, 2 statements).
stances.require: Syllabi at 2 universities say the instructor discloses when and where they use AI (OTHER.c02). At 1 university, the instructional team may ask students for their prompt transcripts when misuse is suspected (CT27.c08).
stances.none: Five of the 6 policies with no position give background facts, each stated by 1 or 2 universities. They include that AI can solve nearly any exercise instantly, so submitted code no longer shows understanding (CT35.c07, 2 universities), and that current coding agents can produce complete projects without human help (CT21.c07, 1 university). Others say that reporting students for cheating is exhausting for the instructor (CT39.c06, 2 universities) and that students flagged for AI use in a previous semester scored lower (CT43.c05, 1 university). The remaining policy says the instructor may talk with a student suspected of misuse before any report (CT39.c04, 1 university).
